entry.title: Inside Microsoft’s BitNet: Ternary Lookup-Table Kernels on CPU and CUDA

link.title: Inside Microsoft’s BitNet: Ternary Lookup-Table Kernels on CPU and CUDA

entry.content:
Two years of quantization work have convinced most teams that 4-bit is the practical floor for running large language models on everyday hardware. Microsoft’s BitNet refuses that floor entirely. Its weights live in {-1, 0, +1}, roughly 1.58 bits each, and the repository we are touring today is the official runtime for them. We looked at what BitNet is back in April in the conceptual overview; this time we walk the source itself, from a HuggingFace checkpoint all the way to lookup-table matrix multiplications executing inside a patched llama.cpp.

The interesting part of this codebase is not the transformers — those are ordinary — but the machinery around them. A build-time code generator emits AVX2 GEMM kernels as C++ text, a conversion tool reorders ternary weights into exactly the layout those kernels want, and a thin C++ shim overrides ggml’s mul_mat so llama.cpp runs BitNet kernels without knowing it. There is also a parallel GPU path where a pure PyTorch model calls hand-written CUDA kernels through ctypes. If you have read our tours of DeepSpeed’s ragged inference engine, TVM’s Relax VM, or Triton, this sits at a very different point on the same spectrum: almost no abstraction, maximal specialization per model shape.

Everything below links to real files on main. Diagrams first, then sections.

The BitNet ternary stack: setup and entry scripts at the left, checkpoint conversion and kernel codegen in the middle, generated AVX2/NEON kernels feeding a patched llama.cpp, with a pure-PyTorch CUDA detour below.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • setup_env.py orchestrates everything once: it quantizes the checkpoint, invokes codegen, and compiles a patched llama.cpp (compile).
  • run_inference.py and run_inference_server.py are thin wrappers that drive the resulting llama-cli and llama-server binaries.
  • convert-hf-to-gguf-bitnet.py packs ternary weights into three on-disk layouts: I2_S, TL1 and TL2.
  • codegen_tl2.py and codegen_tl1.py emit AVX2 and NEON lookup-table kernels; gemm-config.h holds the tiling knobs.
  • The generated headers live in preset_kernels and are included by ggml-bitnet-lut.cpp, the mul_mat override.
  • On GPU, gpu/model.py implements the transformer in PyTorch and calls bitnet_kernels.cu through ctypes.
  • e2e_benchmark.py times the whole thing end to end.

One Checkpoint, Three Layouts

The conversion tool, convert-hf-to-gguf-bitnet.py, is the quiet hero of this repository. It subclasses the llama.cpp GGUF exporter — see the Model base class at line 48 — but its BitnetModel subclass at line 1031 carries a scale_map (line 1077) that matches each linear layer to its precomputed activation scale. Ternary models throw away weight magnitudes, so the activation scales become the only thing keeping the forward pass calibrated; losing one layer’s scale is a silent quality disaster, and the map is how the tool avoids it.

Three output layouts fall out of one pass. The first is I2_S: quantize_to_i2_s maps {-1, 0, 1} to {0, 1, 2} (line 700), packs four ternary values into every byte (lines 705-725), and appends a 32-byte float32 scale tail per superblock. That is the format llama-quantize understands, which is why prepare_model in setup_env.py can finish the job by invoking the stock quantizer with the I2_S ftype (lines 145-152). Clever reuse: BitNet gets a standard GGUF file instead of inventing a container format.

The other two layouts, TL1 and TL2, are not about compression at all — they are about access order. transform_to_tl1 and transform_to_tl2 reorder and re-encode weights so that the lookup-table kernels of the next section can stream them sequentially. The preprocessing helpers (TL1 at line 483, TL2 at line 601) split each weight matrix into the block shapes the generated code will iterate over. If you have ever wondered why you cannot just run the stock gguf through the LUT path, this is why: the weights on disk are pre-shuffled for a specific kernel.

Codegen: Writing AVX2 Kernels at Build Time

Instead of hand-writing SIMD kernels for every supported model, BitNet writes Python that writes C++. codegen_tl2.py is the x86 half. Its gen_tbl_impl emits functions like three_tbl_impl_0 (line 287) — precomputed 256-entry lookup tables where each entry is the dot product of one 8-bit activation chunk with all possible ternary weight patterns. Since a ternary byte only takes 3^9-ish meaningful patterns, a multiply-accumulate chain collapses into table lookups plus integer adds.

The GEMM emitters, three_qgemm_lut and two_qgemm_lut, bake the model’s exact block sizes into the emitted loops, and gen_top_api wraps it all with the ggml_preprocessor glue (line 534) that ggml will call. The per-layer constructors from gen_ctor_code wire kernel selection to layer dimensions. docs/codegen.md shows the knobs: --BM, --BK, --bm control the tiling that gets hard-coded into the emitted loops.

How specific is the output? Compare the checked-in preset TL2 header for the 3B model: it guards itself with GGML_BITNET_X86_TL2, defines BK2 32 (line 24), and opens with hand-managed aligned allocators and _mm256 merge helpers (line 26). Every preset directory in preset_kernels/ is a frozen codegen output for one released model. Meanwhile gemm-config.h supplies compile-time tile constants per ISA — AVX2 gets row block 4, column block 128, parallel 4 (lines 3-10) — with NEON-DOTPROD and portable fallbacks below.

This is the same trade TVM made in our Relax VM tour, just at zero abstraction cost: TVM compiles arbitrary schedules through a compiler stack; BitNet stamps out one template with tuned constants. Less general, dramatically simpler, and for a fixed family of ternary transformer shapes, that simplicity wins.

The ggml mul_mat Override

The generated kernels need a host, and the host is ggml-bitnet-lut.cpp — about two hundred lines of glue that hooks into llama.cpp’s compute graph. Initialization (ggml_bitnet_init) allocates per-tensor extra state, and do_permutate applies a runtime row permutation to the in-memory weights, aligning them with the access pattern the generated loops assume.

Dispatch is guarded twice before any kernel runs. can_mul_mat checks the tensor type and device, and mul_mat_get_wsize computes the exact scratch size the qgemm needs — llama.cpp allocates work buffers once per graph, so this sizing function is what lets the LUT path request a different workspace than the stock matmul would. Only then does mul_mat run: it pulls the packed qlut data (line 107), the lut_scales and lut_biases (lines 108-109) that were stashed during init, and hands everything to the shape-matched generated function. Scales and biases ride along because the lookup tables hold raw integer accumulations; dequantization happens after the adds, in float.

Note what is absent: no dispatcher framework, no backend registry, no plugin API. When we toured ONNX Runtime we counted the layers of indirection between a node and its kernel; here it is one function with an if-chain. The cost is equally clear — the file knows llama.cpp internals intimately, so upstream ggml changes can break it, which is exactly why the repo pins its 3rdparty llama.cpp checkout.

The GPU Detour: Pure PyTorch Plus ctypes

The gpu/ directory is a second, independent implementation. Here the transformer is plain PyTorch — Attention, FeedForward, TransformerBlock built on xformers kernels — except every linear is a BitLinearKernel. Its forward quantizes activations to int8 per token (lines 68-71), then calls bitnet_int8xint2_linear, which loads libbitnet.so via ctypes (line 19) and passes raw data_ptr()s plus the current CUDA stream. No torch extension bindings, no autograd bookkeeping — inference only, and it shows.

The CUDA side mirrors the CPU story at smaller scale. bitnet_kernels.cu exports one C symbol, bitlinear_int8xint2, whose body is a chain of shape checks: each known (M, N, K) launches ladder_int8xint2_kernel with tile parameters chosen offline for that layer’s dimensions (lines 4-33). Weights arrive pre-packed as int8 (four ternary values per byte), so the kernel does its own unpack and int8-times-int2 accumulation, writing bf16 output. setup.py builds it as a bare CUDAExtension.

Around it, FastGen does what torch.compile was built for in our Executorch tour: compile_prefill and compile_generate trace the model into CUDA graphs, then generate_all replays them token by token with a KV cache managed by make_cache. The honest caveat: this path only supports the exact layer shapes hard-coded in the kernel dispatch — feed it an unknown width and the kernel prints a warning and skips the GEMM.

From Install to Your First Model

The intended flow is one command: setup_env.py detects your platform (system_info at line 90), pulls the model (get_model_name at line 93), quantizes it, runs codegen via gen_code, and invokes cmake with your chosen compiler (lines 220-222). After that, run_inference.py defaults to the bundled bitnet_b1_58-3B I2_S gguf with a 2048-token context and temperature 0.8, or you can serve it through run_inference_server.py on localhost:8080. Quality checking is built in too — PerplexityTester scores checkpoints against wikitext, and e2e_benchmark.py wraps timed CLI runs.

Being straight about the limits, because the source is: the generated and preset kernels are shape-pinned, so new model widths require a codegen run (docs/codegen.md shows the TL1 and TL2 invocations) and ideally a tuning sweep with GemmTuner, which searches configurations into kernel_config.ini (generate_configurations at line 262). Batch size 1 is the design point; the CUDA kernels literally check M == 1. And the patched llama.cpp is pinned, not merged — you are building a fork by design.

That trade is the whole point. BitNet buys CPU-side 3B-model inference at interactive speeds by refusing generality everywhere else: weights pre-shuffled on disk, kernels stamped out per model, one entry point that does everything. Compare it with the serving-grade generality of vLLM, the embedding focus of Text Embeddings Inference, the int8 CPU story of faster-whisper, or the self-hosted API surface of LocalAI — BitNet is the narrowest of the family and the only one betting the model format itself on ternary weights. For the conceptual background, start with our first BitNet post; for the other end of the efficiency spectrum, see our inference index.
entry.summary: A source tour of Microsoft's BitNet inference framework: how convert-hf-to-gguf-bitnet packs ternary weights, how codegen_tl2 emits AVX2 lookup-table GEMM kernels, and how a patched llama.cpp executes them on CPU and GPU.

entry.title: Inference Rebuilt for Batching - The Ragged Engine of DeepSpeed Inference v2

link.title: Inference Rebuilt for Batching - The Ragged Engine of DeepSpeed Inference v2

entry.content:
Our first walk of microsoft/DeepSpeed stayed on the training side of the tree: ZeRO’s three sharding stages, the pipe engine’s micro-batch schedules, the launcher that SSHes into clusters, and the accelerator layer that speaks for six hardware vendors. That tour deliberately skipped an entire second codebase hiding under the same roof: deepspeed/inference, and inside it a ground-up rebuild called Inference v2. Serving a trained model is a different computational shape from training it — instead of one big batch of identical-length sequences, a server juggles dozens of half-finished conversations, each with its own prompt length, its own growing KV history, and its own arrival time. Training’s padded tensors waste both memory and arithmetic in that world. The v2 code answers with a data layout it calls ragged: many variable-length sequences packed edge to edge into single tensors, with per-sequence metadata travelling alongside in parallel buffers. As always, this is an educational read of published source on the master branch, Apache 2.0 licensed; the training-side tour covers the modules we now zoom past, and readers comparing serving designs can also see how vLLM and SGLang attack the same problem.

The one-sentence summary: InferenceEngineV2 is the front desk that admits requests, DSStateManager is the ledger that tracks every sequence and every KV block, RaggedBatchWrapper is the crate that packs admitted requests into one GPU-shaped batch, and a registry of swappable DSModules wired to hand-written CUDA kernels does the arithmetic.

Overview of the v2 serving stack: a factory pairs a checkpoint source with a model policy, the engine admits requests through the state manager, ragged batching carries sequences into the Llama model, whose layers are assembled by module heuristics and executed by blocked CUDA kernels.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • build_hf_engine is the public constructor, one call from a Hugging Face model name to a running engine.
  • HuggingFaceCheckpointEngine streams weights from the hub, preferring safetensors, with the file fetch at line 38.
  • InferenceV2Policy is the abstract strategy that knows a model family: how to build it and where every parameter belongs.
  • InferenceEngineV2 exposes put at line 107, query at line 158, and can_schedule at line 184.
  • DSStateManager creates sequences with get_or_create_sequence at line 130 and hands out storage with allocate_blocks at line 203.
  • DSSequenceDescriptor keeps the block list per request, extended by extend_kv_cache at line 235.
  • BlockedKVCache owns the pools, with offload and restore moving blocks to host memory.
  • RaggedBatchWrapper turns sequence descriptors into device buffers via insert_sequence at line 134 and finalize at line 184.
  • Llama2InferenceModel walks embed, transformer layers, and unembed over the ragged batch.
  • DSTransformerModelBase builds every layer through factory methods like make_qkv_layer at line 363.

The front desk: put, query, can_schedule

Three verbs define the engine’s public surface, and each maps to a distinct phase of a request’s life. put is admission: the caller supplies a unique id and a tensor of prompt tokens, and the engine first stages them into a host-side placeholder — PlaceholderSequenceDescriptor records what is coming without touching device memory — then asks the state manager for a real DSSequenceDescriptor and copies tokens into a pinned host buffer so the next forward pass can sweep them up. query is the opposite direction: given a uid and a budget of new tokens and blocks, it reports whether the sequence can run this step and hands back the token slice to feed. The scheduler’s judgment call lives in can_schedule, which walks the candidate uids against two limits — the tracked-sequence cap and the free-block count — and returns a SchedulingResult instead of throwing, so a caller can back off gracefully when the engine is saturated. flush retires a finished conversation, returning its blocks through flush_sequence, and serialize saves the whole warm engine for later reload through build_engine_from_ds_checkpoint.

The ledger underneath is DSStateManager, constructed from a DSStateManagerConfig that fixes how many sequences can be tracked and how many cache groups exist. Memory accounting is deliberately indirect: nothing here stores a KV tensor per sequence. Instead each descriptor remembers integer block ids, and the pools themselves live in BlockedKVCache, one per cache group, shaped as flat block-indexed tensors. Handing out ids is BlockedAllocator, a bookkeeping class whose allocate at line 50 returns a tensor of free indices and whose free at line 74 takes them back — the allocator is the whole memory manager, and its discipline is what makes overflow errors impossible to hide. The cache adds two moves the allocator does not know about: offload copies chosen blocks to host memory to free device room, and restore brings them back when their sequence is rescheduled, with a shape helper called split_kv separating key from value views along the way.

Ragged batches: packing a whole server into four tensors

The batch format is where the design earns its name. A padded batch pads every request to the longest one and computes the padding too; a ragged batch concatenates the actual tokens of all in-flight sequences into a single one-dimensional stream and carries, beside it, a metadata buffer saying where each sequence’s tokens start and stop. RaggedBatchWrapper builds exactly this: insert_sequence appends one descriptor’s tokens and block pointers into preallocated host buffers, and finalize uploads everything with a handful of non-blocking copies, after which the batch exposes parallel device tensors — input_ids, the metadata buffer, tokens-to-sequence maps, and crucially kv_ptrs, a flat tensor of raw pointers into the block pools, one entry per layer and per sequence. That pointer table is the hinge of the whole design: the CUDA kernels never see a Python-side index, they read block ids from the metadata buffer and address the KV pools directly, which is why the same kernel handles any batch composition without recompilation.

Attention then proceeds in blocks. AtomBuilder derives per-head work atoms — fixed-size query-and-key spans — from the batch metadata, and the module calls BlockedFlashAttn with those atoms, out scratch, and the pointer tables; its call signature at line 88 is worth reading as the specification of the whole ragged layout. The sizes are tuned by get_q_block_size per head dimension. The same pattern frames both ends of the network: RaggedEmbeddingKernel gathers embedding rows for the packed token stream, and RaggedLogitsGather copies only the last-token rows of each sequence out for sampling — the unembed GEMM still runs over every hidden state, but the gather that produces logits touches the minimum.

Policies, containers, and a metaclass that checks your weights

Getting a Llama checkpoint into this layout is the job of the policy layer. InferenceV2Policy declares two responsibilities — build_model at line 140 instantiates the model class, and populate_model_parameters at line 189 routes every incoming tensor to the right destination through a ContainerMap that separates transformer-layer containers from the embedding-side one. A metaclass enforces the contract: LayerMetaclass rewrites class construction so that annotated attributes become parameter slots, and its call override at line 150 refuses half-initialized containers — a checkpoint loader cannot silently leave a layer empty. Weights themselves are wrapped as InferenceParameter, a tensor subclass that tracks device residency so a quantized weight still living on CPU is caught at use time rather than at a mysterious kernel crash.

The concrete pair for this tour is the Llama family. Llama2Policy supplies the model class and its container map; Llama2TransformerContainer and Llama2NonTransformerContainer name the per-layer and global weights. The model’s forward at line 199 is refreshingly literal: _forward_embed, then a Python loop calling _forward_transformer_layer once per layer index, then _forward_unembed. All the cleverness is one level down, in DSTransformerModelBase, whose factory methods — make_embedding_layer at line 303, make_qkv_layer at line 363, make_norm_layer at line 579 — consult per-architecture configuration, and whose maybe_allocate_kv at line 436 asks the state manager for blocks before each pass using get_kv_requirements. A sibling base, DSMoETransformerModelBase, adds expert layers through make_moe_layer for Mixtral and Qwen-MoE checkpoints.

DSModules: every organ is swappable

The most transferable idea in the tree is the module contract. DSModuleBase requires each implementation to name itself and answer supports_config — a predicate saying which configurations it can handle. Registration is self-service: subclassing DSModuleRegistryBase enrolls the class via register_module at line 49, so importing an implementation file is enough to make it discoverable. At engine construction, the heuristic pickers — instantiate_attention at line 36, instantiate_linear at line 75, instantiate_pre_norm at line 158, plus their embed, unembed, and MoE siblings — walk the registered implementations in priority order and take the first that supports the requested configuration. The shipped set shows the spectrum: DSDenseBlockedAttention builds atoms with build_atoms at line 139 before its forward at line 152; BlasFPLinear is the honest pure-GEMM fallback for unquantized weights; DSPreRMSCUDAModule fuses RMSNorm; DSRaggedEmbedding and DSRaggedUnembed bracket the stream. Anyone adding a model family follows a documented recipe — the AddingAModel guide in the same folder — and anyone adding a faster kernel only has to satisfy the same config predicate, which is exactly how this tree wants extensions to arrive.

From Install to Your First Model

Install with pip install deepspeed, then the v2 path is three lines of Python: from deepspeed.inference.v2.engine_factory import build_hf_engine; engine = build_hf_engine("meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-hf"); engine.put(0, tokens). Between those lines, the factory loads the checkpoint streaming class, builds the policy, populates every container, wraps the model in InferenceEngineV2, and returns an object whose put/query/flush verbs are the entire API. Be honest about the fine print, because the code is: the v2 engine is marked experimental in its own docs, the blocked CUDA kernels target NVIDIA tensor-core GPUs, and running with tensor parallelism greater than one is the configuration the engine actually exercises — single-GPU mode works through the BLAS linear module but is not the optimized path. Quantized-weight support exists in the cutlass GEMM kernels but the coverage of bit-widths is narrower than the training side’s optimizer zoo, and there is no continuous-batching scheduler loop shipped as a runnable daemon — the engine provides put/query/can_schedule and expects your serving loop to call them, unlike the turnkey HTTP servers this series has met in lmdeploy and local inference servers. What you get in exchange is the clearest executable specification of ragged serving we have read: four trees of code where every tensor has a declared owner. Compare the training half at our first DeepSpeed tour, the quantized-kernel approach of Triton, the execution-plan machinery of ONNX Runtime, the mobile side of ExecuTorch, and the speech sibling faster-whisper — the same lesson repeats: production inference is bookkeeping with arithmetic inside.
entry.summary: A second source tour of microsoft/DeepSpeed, this time through the inference half of the tree: the v2 engine factory and its put/query scheduling surface, the ragged manager that tracks sequences in block-sized KV pools, the RaggedBatchWrapper that packs variable-length requests into one CUDA-shaped batch, the policy and container machinery that loads Llama checkpoints without PyTorch modules, and the DSModule registry that swaps every transformer organ for a fused kernel.

entry.title: From Export to Bare Metal - The .pte Path Through pytorch/executorch

link.title: From Export to Bare Metal - The .pte Path Through pytorch/executorch

entry.content:
Every framework we have toured in this series — Triton for kernels, vLLM for throughput, MLC for cross-platform compilation — assumes you have an operating system, a Python runtime, and memory to spare. ExecuTorch, PyTorch’s edge sibling, drops all three assumptions: its target machines are microcontrollers, DSPs, and phone NPUs where your whole model must fit into a memory budget you declare in advance. The price of that constraint shapes every file in the repository, and it produces one of the cleanest ideas in inference engineering: the allocation plan is computed at export time, on a machine that has plenty of RAM, and shipped inside the artifact itself. The runtime never allocates a tensor at inference — it replays a script. This tour follows a .pte file end to end: the exir export flow that partitions, plans, and serializes it; the loader that memory-maps it; the Method that executes it one step at a time; the backend contract that hands subgraphs to vendor libraries; and the LLM runner that turns all of it into a chat loop. As always, this is an educational read of published source on the main branch, under the BSD-style license.

What makes the design worth studying is how much it refuses to do at runtime. There is no scheduler, no batcher, no memory arena hunting for blocks mid-inference — all of that was decided by a Python pass with the whole graph in view. The C++ side stays small enough to read in an afternoon, which is exactly the point for software that ships inside hearing aids and drones.

Overview of the .pte path: exir partitioners carve subgraphs to backends, the memory-planning pass assigns every tensor a spec, serialize_for_executorch writes the flatbuffer, Program loads it, Method replays the plan through the BackendInterface, and the Module plus LLM runner wrap it into an application.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • partitioner.py defines the abstract Partitioner whose call at line 66 runs partition at 75 and returns a PartitionResult with lowered subgraphs.
  • memory_planning_pass.py is where allocation becomes data: MemoryPlanningPass runs at line 280 with a multi-method variant at 346.
  • memory_planning.py computes lifetimes with update_all_tensors_lifetime and validates them through verify_storage_reuse at 165.
  • _serialize.py is the exit door: serialize_for_executorch writes the flatbuffer program and its external data segments.
  • program.cpp is the loader: Program::load verifies the file, num_methods at 353 counts entry points, and load_method at 384 builds a Method.
  • method_meta.cpp reports what a method needs — input shapes, output shapes, memory plan sizes.
  • method.cpp is the engine: Method::init wires kernels and delegates once, step at 1723 and execute at 1780 replay the plan.
  • interface.h is the vendor contract: BackendInterface with init at 84 and execute at 99.
  • module.cpp is the friendly C++ API: Module::load picks a DataLoader strategy, load_method at 543 prepares an entry point.
  • text_llm_runner.cpp is a complete chat loop: generate drives prefill at 284 and per-token decode.
  • text_decoder_runner.cpp runs one method step per token through the sampler.
  • memory_allocator.h and hierarchical_allocator.h are the bump allocators that hold every planned buffer.

Export: edge dialect, delegates, and a plan for every byte

The Python half of the repo answers a question most runtimes answer with heuristics at load time: how much memory does this model need, and where does each tensor sit? The flow starts with torch.export and a descent into the edge dialect — operator decompositions that rewrite ATen ops into the edge subset with explicit dtype and layout. Then partitioning: a backend implements the Partitioner interface, declares which ops it supports, and the exporter slices matching subgraphs out of the graph, wrapping each in a lowered module that the backend compiles however it likes. Whatever the backend cannot claim stays as a portable-kernel subgraph, so a Core ML or QNN delegate can sit beside reference C++ kernels in the same method.

The distinctive part is the planning pass. MemoryPlanningPass walks the traced graph, and for every node that materializes a tensor it attaches an allocation spec at line 229 — size, dtype, alignment, and a lifetime computed from when the tensor is last read. The core machinery in memory_planning.py collects specs from nodes, then solves a two-dimensional packing problem: tensors whose lifetimes do not overlap can share one buffer, and update_all_tensors_lifetime at line 548 supplies the intervals the packer needs. The result is a set of named memory plans — each a fixed-size pool with fixed offsets — and a verifier at line 165 that refuses to emit a program whose planned buffers overlap in invalid ways. Serialization then writes the whole story into the .pte: the flatbuffer program from serialize_for_executorch at line 44 plus constant segments laid out so a device can consume them directly. It is the same precompute-everything philosophy we saw in ONNX Runtime’s planners in the onnxruntime-2 tour, taken to its logical endpoint: not cached per input signature, but baked into the file.

Loading: segments, verification, and zero-copy

The C++ half begins with Program::load, and its first act is paranoia. The loader checks the flatbuffer identifier, verifies the whole buffer with a flatbuffers verifier, parses the extended header, and only then hands back a Program. The file is organized as segments — program, constants, mutable data — described by segment info records, and the loader never copies them: it keeps a pointer into whatever the DataLoader provided, which can be a file read, an mmap, or memory embedded at link time. PteDataMap indexes the named data so constants land where the plan expects. A Program can hold several methods — the LLM use case compiles prefill and decode as separate entry points — enumerated by num_methods at line 353 and get_method_name at 364, each loaded independently through load_method at 384, which consults method_meta for the shapes and plan sizes it must reserve.

Execution: one method, one step, one delegate call

Method::init at line 937 is where the plan meets real memory. The caller supplies a hierarchical allocator — a stack of named pools sized exactly as the export promised — and init carves every planned buffer out of those pools without a single dynamic allocation. It then walks the graph’s instructions: portable kernels are resolved by name against the registered kernel library, and each delegated subgraph is initialized through the backend’s init at line 84, which compiles the subgraph into an opaque DelegateHandle. From there, execution is a replay: Method::step at line 1723 copies inputs into their planned slots, execute at 1780 walks the instruction list — kernel calls through the EValue variant, or execute at line 99 on the backend for delegated spans — and every write lands in memory whose address was decided in Python. The TensorParser is the quiet workhorse mapping feed tensors onto the planned buffers, and the optional EventTracer records per-op spans when profiling is compiled in. The Module layer above smooths the ergonomics — its constructors at line 125 choose between FileDataLoader and mmap variants depending on the platform — and BundledModule goes one step further by linking the .pte into the application binary itself, which is how a watch face model ships with no filesystem at all.

Two supporting pieces make this machinery survivable on real hardware. The first is the DataLoader abstraction: because the loader only ever hands out borrowed views — the FreeableBuffer type wraps a pointer plus a destructor — the same Method code runs against a heap read on a laptop and against flash-mapped memory on an RTOS without caring which. The Module constructors pick the strategy per platform, trying mmap first and falling back to file reads where it is unavailable. The second is the Result type, which replaces exceptions with a value-or-error pattern throughout the runtime: every loader call, init call, and step returns one, and the absence of exception machinery keeps the binary small enough for the MCUs this code targets. Neither piece is glamorous, but together they are why the executor compiles with almost no standard library dependency — an explicit design goal you can feel in every header.

From Install to Your First Model

The LLM path ties the pieces together. TextLLMRunner owns two methods from one .pte — prefill and decode — and generate at line 74 runs prefill at 284 in chunks sized to the device, then loops TextDecoderRunner::step at line 40, which executes the decode method once, samples, appends the token, and invokes the callback. Nothing here batches across users — the whole design targets one conversation on one device, which is why the runner can stay a few hundred lines.

After pip install executorch, the knobs worth knowing are the memory ones: memory-planning modes choose between contiguous pools and per-plan pools, --memory-planning output can be inspected as a text layout, and backends like XNNPACK or Core ML register themselves as partitioners you add to the export call. Honest limits: we read the loader and method hot path, not the kernel libraries or the vendor delegates — the QNN and Core ML trees are large projects of their own. We benchmarked nothing; the zero-copy claims are structural, and real devices add alignment surprises that the dim-order passes only partially hide. And the executor is single-threaded by design — parallelism exists only inside backends. Compared with OpenVINO and ONNX Runtime, which carry their allocators and schedulers into the runtime, ExecuTorch’s answer is radical precomputation: the .pte is not just a model format, it is a memory map — and that is why the smallest devices in this series run it.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of pytorch/executorch along the whole life of a .pte file: the exir partitioners and memory-planning pass that pre-compute every tensor's address at export time, the serialized flatbuffer with its segments, Program's zero-copy loader, Method's init-once execute-per-step loop, the BackendInterface delegate contract, and the Module and LLM runner layers on top.

entry.title: Inside the Seek Loop - Timestamps, Fallback, and Hallucination Guards in SYSTRAN/faster-whisper

link.title: Inside the Seek Loop - Timestamps, Fallback, and Hallucination Guards in SYSTRAN/faster-whisper

entry.content:
Our first walk of SYSTRAN/faster-whisper introduced the cast: WhisperModel, the batched wrapper, PyAV audio, the Silero VAD, and the claim that a reimplementation on CTranslate2 makes the same model four times faster. What that tour did not open up is transcribe.py’s engine room — the eighteen hundred lines where the actual decoding decisions live. Whisper’s own implementation is famously a pile of heuristics: a seek pointer that sometimes advances and sometimes retries, three separate tests for whether a decoded window can be trusted, a prompt manager that keeps context coherent across windows, and a timestamp alignment scheme that reads cross-attention maps. faster-whisper rebuilds every one of those heuristics in Python over CTranslate2’s primitives, and reading them is a masterclass in production speech recognition. As always, this is an educational read of published source on the master branch, MIT-licensed; the first post covers the module map we now zoom past.

The one-sentence summary: generate_segments is a clock, generate_with_fallback is a skeptic, and the VAD is the map that tells both where speech actually is. Everything else in the package exists to feed, verify, or measure that trio.

Overview of the decoding machinery: the package surface hands audio through the VAD into WhisperModel, whose seek loop and fallback logic drive CTranslate2; the batched wrapper reuses the same pieces over merged chunks, while benchmarks, tests, and the Docker entry measure and package it all.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • transcribe.py holds the whole engine: WhisperModel with its public transcribe at line 781.
  • The seek loop is generate_segments, and its clip arithmetic starts at line 1176.
  • generate_with_fallback decides whether a window’s output can be trusted.
  • add_word_timestamps rebuilds word timing from the align call at line 1746.
  • The batched wrapper is the batched sibling, with its own transcribe at line 254.
  • vad.py supplies get_speech_timestamps and collect_chunks at 220.
  • audio.py decodes any container through PyAV with decode_audio and pad_or_trim at 117.
  • utils.py fetches converted checkpoints via download_model and formats timestamps at line 118.
  • speed_benchmark.py measures real-time factor with measure_speed; wer_benchmark.py scores accuracy.

The seek loop: windows, clips, and silence

The public transcribe builds the option dataclasses — TranscriptionOptions at line 71 carries every knob — and then hands you a generator, which is where generate_segments begins. Its unit of work is the thirty-second window. Without a VAD, the seek pointer marches through the file in 30-second steps; with one, the loop first asks get_speech_timestamps for speech regions and converts them into seek clips, so the pointer jumps from speech to speech and silence never reaches the model. The per-window bookkeeping is precise: time_offset at line 1205 converts the seek index into seconds via the feature extractor’s per-frame time, the mel features are sliced to the window, and everything decoded is stamped relative to that offset. After a window is accepted, the seek advances past the last timestamp token rather than the full window — the original Whisper’s trick for not losing audio between timestamp boundaries.

The most interesting branch is the hallucination guard. Whisper’s known failure mode is inventing fluent text over silence or music — famously “Thank you for watching” loops. When hallucination_silence_threshold is set and a segment looks suspicious, the code at lines 1327 through 1369 uses the word timestamps to find where speech actually resumed, truncates the seek to the last real word end, and re-decodes just the silence-free remainder. Note the dependency: the guard needs word timestamps to work, which is why the option is disabled by default and why the docstring ties the two together. The VAD path also patches timestamps back into wall-clock positions through SpeechTimestampsMap, because chunks were removed and re-ordered and every segment’s reported time must land in the original audio’s frame of reference.

generate_with_fallback: deciding a window is wrong

generate_with_fallback is the skeptic that sits between the encoder and your transcript. It samples with the first temperature, then runs three tests on the result. The first is repetitiveness: get_compression_ratio at line 1924 zlib-compresses the text, and if the ratio above the threshold says the output is too repetitive, needs_fallback is set at line 1520. The second is confidence: if the average log probability at line 1533 falls under log_prob_threshold, the window is rejected. The third is the clever one — if there is no speech in the window at all, the low-probability result is explicitly accepted at line 1550, because “silence” is a correct answer for silence, and punishing it would cause the fallback loop to hallucinate something to say. On failure, the temperature climbs — up to len(temperatures) retries, each with best_of sampling at line 1473 — and the best surviving candidate wins. Before any of this runs, get_suppressed_tokens at line 1929 assembles the suppression list: non-speech tokens, user-supplied suppressions, and the compression-ratio flagged set. The prompt machinery at line 1569 closes the loop across windows, extending the previous window’s text so the model keeps its style and vocabulary — sot_sequence and task tokens included.

Word timestamps: alignment from CTranslate2

Word timestamps in this codebase are not heuristic guesswork — they are cross-attention arithmetic delegated to CTranslate2. add_word_timestamps at line 1604 collects the text tokens per segment and calls find_alignment at line 1735, which invokes model.align at line 1746 — CTranslate2 runs the DTW over cross-attention maps with a median filter, and returns token-to-frame alignments plus per-token probabilities. The Python side then does the cleanup Whisper’s original is known for: a median-based duration cap at lines 1630 through 1653 truncates impossible word lengths at sentence boundaries, merge_punctuations at line 1955 glues punctuation back onto neighbors, and the tokenizer’s split_to_word_tokens handles scripts where words do not split on spaces — CJK among them. The same alignment data feeds the timestamp-based splitter at line 1061, which cuts long segments at reliable timestamp tokens when multilingual subtitles demand it, and detect_language at line 1811 reuses the encoder output for its language-likelihood pass.

The batched sibling and the VAD that feeds it

The speed story closes with the batched wrapper class at line 111. Its transcribe at line 254 asks the VAD for speech regions, then collect_chunks at line 220 reassembles them into batch_size windows of 30 seconds each — padding partial chunks — and forward at line 119 runs one CTranslate2 batch over all of them. Per-window decoding inside the batch is generate_segment_batched at line 174, which skips the fallback machinery for speed and returns logits-level results that the wrapper scores and trims at line 246. The results finally stream through _batched_segments_generator at line 582, where chunk offsets are restored to original-audio time — the same restore_speech_timestamps helper at line 1889 the non-batched path uses. The trade the README’s seventeen-seconds benchmark makes is now legible: batching and VAD pruning replace the fallback skeptic with a cheaper pass, and the Silero model itself at line 330 runs as a bundled ONNX file — the same runtime-engine pattern ONNX Runtime standardized, applied to a 2-megabyte gatekeeper.

Two support modules deserve their paragraph because both are quieter than they look. The feature extractor computes log-Mel spectrograms, and _get_feature_kwargs at line 763 quietly checks the model directory for a preprocessor config so that older converted checkpoints keep their original mel parameters instead of silently drifting — a two-line guard against one of the nastiest classes of silent accuracy bugs. The tokenizer wraps Hugging Face’s tokenizers library with Whisper’s task and language token bookkeeping, and its word-splitting logic is what makes CJK and mixed-script timestamps work at all. Around the package, the Docker entry point wires a wav file to a model with nothing but environment variables, and test_utils.py covers the download layer — including the resume-from-partial-download behavior that anyone on hotel Wi-Fi will eventually thank.

From Install to Your First Model

Everything above activates through arguments to transcribe(): vad_filter=True arms the VAD path, word_timestamps=True enables the alignment machinery, and hallucination_silence_threshold (a float in seconds) arms the guard — which requires word timestamps. The benchmark directory is the honest way to see the trade-offs: speed_benchmark.py sweeps model sizes and batch settings, memory_benchmark.py tracks peak memory per compute type, and wer_benchmark.py scores the accuracy cost of batching, with shared dataset helpers behind them.

Honest limits: this walk stayed in Python; the actual Transformer math is CTranslate2’s, and its align internals are a separate engine we did not read. The hallucination guard’s thresholds are heuristics tuned on English-ish audio — other languages may need different values, and the code itself warns that the timestamp trick assumes VAD quality. We read, not measured: the README’s numbers come from the benchmark files, not from us. And the fallback logic is deliberately conservative — turning all three guards off is a legitimate speed choice for clean single-speaker audio, as the tests in test_transcribe.py demonstrate with real fixtures. For context in this series: vLLM and SGLang batch text tokens across users, LocalAI and xorbitsai/inference wrap speech models behind the same server walls as LLMs, and OpenVINO quantizes the same Whisper architecture for CPU. faster-whisper’s lesson — guard the clock, trust the alignment, batch only what the VAD proves is speech — is the most transferable of the lot.
entry.summary: A second source tour of SYSTRAN/faster-whisper, this time inside the decoding mechanics: generate_segments' seek bookkeeping across VAD clips, generate_with_fallback's three failure tests, suppressed-token filtering, the CTranslate2 cross-attention alignment behind word timestamps, the batched sibling's chunk merging, and the benchmark harnesses that measure it all.

entry.title: FlashInfer Source Tour: The Plan/Run Machine Behind Fast Attention

link.title: FlashInfer Source Tour: The Plan/Run Machine Behind Fast Attention

entry.content:
Every time you chat with a model served by vLLM or SGLang, there is a good chance the attention step was executed by FlashInfer. The library sits one layer below the engines: engines decide what to run, FlashInfer decides how a batch of ragged, differently-lengthed requests gets turned into a handful of well-shaped CUDA launches. We toured the compiler side of this world with Triton and the raw kernel side with FlashAttention; FlashInfer is the connective tissue between the two, and its source is a masterclass in an API style that deserves more attention than it gets: plan once, then run many times.

The reason for that style is structural. A decode step over a paged KV cache cannot be described by tensor shapes alone — it depends on sequence lengths, page tables, and how much scratch memory the GPU can spare. FlashInfer’s answer is a two-phase contract: a plan() call inspects all of that on the CPU, picks a schedule, allocates workspaces, and records a plan; a run() call then launches the prepared kernel with almost no host-side branching. In this tour we follow that contract through the wrappers, the host-side scheduler, the JIT kernel modules, the paged KV machinery, and the autotuner that quietly picks which compiled variant to trust.

The FlashInfer stack: plan/run wrappers at the top, host-side planning and JIT module loading in the middle, split-KV CUDA kernels below, with the AutoTuner steering tactic choices.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • BatchDecodeWithPagedKVCacheWrapper and BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper are the two workhorse classes every engine talks to.
  • Their plan methods consult the host-side DecodePlan scheduler before any GPU work happens.
  • get_batch_decode_module and get_batch_prefill_module load or JIT-compile the actual kernel binaries.
  • The kernels live in headers: decode.cuh and prefill.cuh.
  • page.py and page.cuh handle writing new tokens into the paged cache.
  • AutoTuner benchmarks candidate tactics per shape and caches the winners.

The Plan/Run Contract

Open decode.py and the wrapper reads like a state machine. plan() takes the whole batch description — sequence lengths, page table indirection, kv cache layout — and returns nothing you can multiply; what it returns is a filled workspace and a plan info blob. Then run() (line 2787) does the real launch with the arguments the plan froze. The split exists because engines like vLLM run many decode steps against an unchanged batch structure: paying the scheduling cost once per step instead of once per token is the whole point.

The prefill side mirrors it in BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper. Its plan has more to decide — query lengths vary per request, custom masks are allowed, and ragged (non-paged) KV is supported too — while run stays thin. There is also a single-request convenience path, single_prefill_with_kv_cache, for workloads that never batch.

One subclass shows why this design survives production: CUDAGraphBatchDecodeWithPagedKVCacheWrapper exists so the same decode step can be captured into a CUDA graph. Graph replay forbids host-side decisions at launch time, which is exactly what the plan/run split guarantees — after plan(), run() is deterministic enough to record.

The plan phase is also where backend selection happens, and the source is unusually transparent about it. On the prefill side, get_fmha_module loads the canonical cuDNN-free FMHA modules, while get_customize_batch_prefill_module exposes a mechanism for callers to register their own kernel modules under a name the wrapper can resolve later. Engines exploit this to swap in architecture-specific kernels without forking the wrapper code. The plan call resolves which module actually fits the current dtype, head dimension, and device — so a vLLM deployment on Hopper and one on Blackwell can run identical Python while hitting completely different binaries underneath.

Planning on the Host, Executing on the Device

The scheduler is where the interesting arithmetic lives, and it is pure C++ in scheduler.cuh. Decode work per request is proportional to its KV length, so the scheduler partitions the KV dimension into chunks and assigns chunks to thread blocks — the split-KV strategy FlashAttention popularized, but computed per batch on the host rather than baked into the kernel. DecodePlanImpl walks batch sizes against the available smem and registers budget, producing a DecodePlanInfo (struct at line 366) that later serializes into a plain int64 vector — deliberately boring, deliberately stable.

Prefill planning needs a search instead of a partition, because a single long request can dominate a batch. PrefillBinarySearchKVChunkSize binary-searches the largest KV chunk that still fills the GPU, balancing load across requests of wildly different lengths. The elegance here is that all of this is host code compiled into the Python extension — no separate scheduler service, no graph compiler, just a well-tested C++ function the wrapper calls before every fresh batch.

The Paged KV Cache Layer

Engines do not store KV contiguously; they store it as pages in a pool so sequences can grow without reallocation. FlashInfer accepts that layout as ground truth. On the Python side, page.py builds batch indices and positions from the page indirection, and append_paged_kv_cache is the entry point engines call after every generated token. There is a parallel MLA variant (append_paged_mla_kv_cache) for the compressed latent layout DeepSeek models use.

The CUDA side is refreshingly small for how load-bearing it is: AppendPagedKVCacheKernel and its decode-specialized twin (line 363) copy new K/V rows into their page slots, handling the case where one token’s data straddles a page boundary. This is unglamorous code, but it is the boundary contract between an engine’s memory manager and FlashInfer’s kernels — get it wrong and every downstream attention result is silently wrong.

Newer hardware brings a twist: writing the cache can be fused with quantizing it. nvfp4_quantize_append_paged_kv_cache and its CUDA counterpart (NVFP4QuantizeAppendPagedKVCache at line 621) quantize incoming FP16/BF16 tensors to NVFP4 blocks during the append itself, halving cache traffic on Blackwell-class GPUs without a separate quantization launch. The same trick exists for the MLA layout. It is a small example of a big theme: on modern accelerators, memory movement is the compute budget, so FlashInfer keeps collapsing separate memory passes into the ops that were touching the data anyway.

One Kernel Family, Many Backends

FlashInfer is often described as “one library,” but the source shows a family. The canonical headers compile per (head_dim, dtype, pos-encoding) combination through the JIT path: get_batch_decode_module checks a cache, and on miss invokes nvcc through the jit/ machinery to produce a .so for exactly your shapes. First call is slow; every call after is a dlopen away.

Beyond the canonical kernels sit the vendor paths. trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache routes to NVIDIA’s trtllm-gen kernels — the ones behind TensorRT-LLM — while xqa_batch_decode_with_kv_cache exposes the XQA kernel, and fast_decode_plan is the planner that understands when each of these backends is eligible. The decode dispatcher in decode.cuh shows the same pattern inside a single backend: the standard kernel (line 624) for GQA shapes, and a dedicated MLA kernel (line 910) when the cache is in DeepSeek’s compressed layout. Prefill mirrors all of it in prefill.cuh with a ragged-KV twin at line 4799.

If you read our ONNX Runtime tour, this is the same “many execution providers, one API” idea rebuilt for attention — except here the provider choice happens per batch at plan time, not per model at load time.

Cascades, Merges, and the Autotuner

Two quieter subsystems round out the library. The first is cascade attention: when thousands of requests share a long system prompt, recomputing attention over the shared prefix per request is waste. MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper runs attention once per prefix level and then merges the partial results — because attention outputs with their log-sum-exp statistics form a mathematically clean algebra, merging two partial attentions is exact, not approximate. The merge kernels in cascade.cuh (batched version at line 220, persistent variant at line 374) implement that algebra on-device, and the Python side exposes it through merge_state and the in-place merge_state_in_place.

The second is the AutoTuner (class at line 1535). Many kernels have several valid tactics — tile choices, split counts — and which one wins depends on your exact shapes. The tuner wraps tunable ops, profiles each tactic the first time a shape appears (TuningConfig and DynamicTensorSpec describe the shape buckets), and persists winners to disk so the cost is paid once per machine. vLLM and SGLang both flip it on in production; it is the difference between “FlashInfer is fast” and “FlashInfer is fast on your shapes.”

From Install to Your First Decode

Getting started is pip install flashinfer-python plus a CUDA 12+ toolkit for the JIT path. A minimal decode loop follows the contract directly: allocate a workspace buffer, construct BatchDecodeWithPagedKVCacheWrapper, call plan() with your float and int workspaces, then call run() per step. Auxiliary ops follow the same pattern — rope kernels for positional encoding, and a full sampling family in sampling.cuh (top-k, top-p, min-p kernels) so engines never round-trip sampling through slow fallbacks.

Being honest about the limits, because the source is: the JIT path needs a working nvcc at runtime, so first-plan latency on a fresh shape can be seconds — autotuning multiplies that if you enable it cold. The MLA and FP8/FP4 paths are tuned for specific architectures, and the attention core shows the API still migrating between the classic wrappers and newer module forms, which means engine integrations pin versions carefully. This is infrastructure that assumes you run an engine, not a chat app.

That positioning is what makes the source worth reading. llama.cpp sells portability by avoiding CUDA abstractions; MLC and TVM compile everything ahead of time; FlashInfer sits deliberately in between — ahead-of-time architecture, just-in-time kernels, per-batch planning, and an autotuner closing the loop. For the bigger picture of where it sits among serving stacks, see the inference index, and for the engine that consumes it most visibly, the vLLM tour.
entry.summary: A source tour of FlashInfer, the kernel library behind vLLM and SGLang: the plan/run wrapper contract, host-side split-KV scheduling, JIT-compiled decode and prefill kernels, paged KV cache appends, cascade merges, and the AutoTuner.

entry.title: Inside TurboMind: The C++ Engine Core of InternLM/lmdeploy

link.title: Inside TurboMind: The C++ Engine Core of InternLM/lmdeploy

entry.content:
Our first visit to InternLM/lmdeploy stayed above the waterline: the CLI, the lite quantization toolkit, the OpenAI-compatible server, and the fork where a request picks either the readable PyTorch engine or the compiled TurboMind core. This visit goes under the waterline, into the C++ half that EuroSys-grade numbers were built on. The questions here are the classic serving-engine questions — where do requests wait, who decides what runs next, how are KV-cache pages handed out and reused — answered with a design that is unusually clean: one engine thread that owns all mutable state, a scheduler that plans several steps ahead of the GPU, and a two-level block system where logical sequences borrow from pooled physical pages. As always, this is an educational walk through published source, Apache-2.0 licensed, on the main branch.

The design decision everything else hangs on is single-threaded ownership. Instead of locks sprinkled through the request path, TurboMind gives the engine one internal thread that pops from a Gateway, and everything else — Python, signal delivery, result forwarding — talks to that thread through queues. Reading the loop below is therefore the most direct way to understand the whole system.

The TurboMind core: the Python TurboMind class reaches through the _turbomind pybind module into the Engine; requests arrive via the Gateway, the Engine's internal thread validates, accepts, cancels and retires them, the Scheduler plans against block pools and a prefix trie, and the ModelExecutor consumes prepared BatchData on its own thread.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The Python side is TurboMind: it loads weights, calls _create_engine, and hands out per-stream instances from create_instance.
  • The boundary is a pybind module: PYBIND11_MODULE exposes engine handles, request structs, and even multimodal inputs, with config classes auto-generated via a for_each trick at line 379.
  • Gateway is the doorsill: push and pop for requests, cancel for aborts, and a dedicated signal thread so notifications never block the caller.
  • The engine loop at Engine::Impl::InternalThreadEntry is the whole scheduling brain in one while-true.
  • The Scheduler plans each step: admission, prefix matching, resume versus continue, publication.
  • Blocks live in two pools — CacheBlock physical pages managed by CacheBlockPool, and LogicalBlock sequences that borrow them.

The bridge and the boundaries

Between Python and C++ sits more than a translator. The bind.cpp module defines three worlds: engine handles, the request vocabulary — requests, sequences, signals, multimodal inputs — and configuration. The configuration part is the most elegant: C++ config structs register their own fields, so a helper at lines 379 through 390 can expose every option to Python without a hand-written def per attribute — add a field to the struct and the binding follows. Multimodal inputs get first-class treatment too, with per-model item types such as QwenVitItem carrying grid dimensions and token spans, and tensor data crossing by dlpack capsule rather than by copy. On the Python side, TurboMind.init resolves the model source, _process_weights and _create_weight move tensors into the layout the kernels expect, and runtime weight updates or sleep/wakeup travel the same bridge through update_params and wakeup.

The Gateway deserves a closer look because it is the only object on the hot path that Python threads touch concurrently. push enqueues a request and wakes the signal thread; pop drains it under a free-slot budget, optionally blocking; notify is how the engine thread talks back — signals for finished, failed, or cancelled requests are handed to a separate signal thread so that a slow consumer of results never stalls the engine loop itself. Cancellation is also asynchronous: cancel marks a request, and the engine observes it in its own time, which is why the loop below has an explicit Cancel step rather than an interrupt.

The engine loop, one thread to rule the batch

InternalThreadEntry starts with pinning chores — CUDA device, a stream, allocators — then enters the loop that is the engine. Only rank zero talks to the Gateway: the pop at line 797 requests as many free slots as the batch can offer and blocks only when the batch is completely empty, a detail that keeps idle GPUs from spinning hot. The popped requests pass Validate, which checks everything the scheduler would otherwise discover mid-step — token limits, session resumption, multimodal payload shapes — and rejects early with per-request signals. Tensor-parallel ranks then synchronize at line 804 only when the batch is empty, and the full request set is broadcast so every rank runs the identical step.

The body of the iteration is a fixed order that reads like a checklist: Accept turns validated requests into sequences, Cancel applies aborts, gateway notify flushes the resulting signals, Retire frees finished sequences, and only then — with the active count re-reduced across data-parallel groups — does Schedule run. Two quiet guardians follow: FailStalledHeadOfLine catches the case where a queue head cannot fit and everything behind it starves, and cache-stats logging is throttled so observability never becomes load. The ordering matters: because retire precedes schedule, freed pages are reusable in the very same step.

The Scheduler: admission, prefixes, and partial siblings

Where the engine loop is a metronome, the Scheduler is the strategist. Each pass builds a ScheduleState and walks three phases. Required admission at line 1105 handles sequences already holding resources; optional admission at line 1219 brings new prompts in only if that cannot hurt anyone admitted. Prompt admission itself is where the KV cache gets interesting: AdmitPrompt ensures the sequence has blocks, then MatchPrompt walks the prompt against the prefix trie to find already-materialized blocks, and IndexMissingBlocks decides what must still be computed.

The subtle machinery is for shared and resumed sequences. PlanResume rehydrates a sequence from a stored session, SetupPartialSiblings splits a shared prefix where two requests diverge mid-block, and a trio — SetProducers, CheckProducers, MarkProduced — tracks which in-flight sequence will fill a block that others want, so cache reuse does not have to wait for a sequence to finish. Publication of checkpoint blocks is planned separately at PlanPublication, with a clamp that keeps a forward pass from outrunning its context. The step ends with ReplayMemory applying the plan to the block system and CommitResults handing tokens back.

Underneath the scheduler sits a small object system with real engineering in it. A LogicalBlockPtr and a CacheBlockPtr are reference-counted handles that know their pools, so release paths are exception-safe by construction. The physical pool answers the classic eviction question cheaply: SortedBlocks produces candidates in reuse-friendly order, and a Stamp computed over a set of blocks gives the trie a fingerprint to index. Lifecycle is explicit rather than implicit: Invalidate drops a block whose owner rewrote it, Deallocate returns memory to the allocator, and the logical pool’s Recycle fires the trie-erase callback that keeps the prefix index honest — the comment there even notes the pool deliberately stays prefix-agnostic.

The detail view: Python frontend and pybind bridge on the left; the engine tier of Gateway, engine loop, request structs, and BatchData; the scheduler tier with block pools, the prefix trie, and the block implementation file; the memory layer of pages and slabs underneath; and the ModelExecutor thread on the right.

Walking the detail diagram, a token’s journey touches every tier. The request struct itself is compact — Request carries inputs and a generation config, Sequence is the long-lived state, and CacheCopy records when a shared physical block must be duplicated before divergence. The block pools are pooled twice over: LogicalBlockPool recycles logical objects through a callback that erases the sequence from the prefix trie on recycle, while physical pages come from PageAllocator and the pool storage itself is slab-allocated so steady-state serving never wakes the general-purpose heap. On the other end, ModelExecutor runs its own internal thread with a Run that consumes the BatchData the engine filled — container structs like ResolvedCopy carry the block copies that must happen before attention reads.

Splitting the engine thread from the executor thread is not ceremony; it is latency hiding. The scheduler can plan step N+1 — including block allocation and copies — while the GPU is still finishing step N inside the model, and the two only meet at the BatchData hand-off. The same separation protects the reverse path: interrupts such as Interrupt mark a sequence for the engine to observe at a step boundary, and Finalize runs cleanup once the executor has drained, so a cancelled request never frees memory that attention kernels are still reading. It is the same discipline that made the single-threaded engine safe in the first place, applied one layer down.

From Install to Your First Model

Install is pip install lmdeploy, then lmdeploy serve api_server <model> picks TurboMind by default. What this tour adds is the operational reading: create_instance per stream is cheap because the engine, not the instance, owns state; the schedule metrics surfaced by get_schedule_metrics are the engine’s own counters about admission and cache pressure, worth watching before raising max_batch_size; and prefix reuse is automatic — the trie and producer tracking above are why repeated system prompts do not multiply prefill cost.

Honest limits: this walk covered the orchestration core, not the kernels — attention, MoE, and the linear layers under models/llama are their own mountain, and the PyTorch engine shares none of this C++ machinery. We read, not benchmarked; the design claims here are structural. And the engine thread model is a real contract: user code that blocks inside callbacks stalls the whole batch, which is precisely why the Gateway keeps its signal thread. For placement in the ecosystem, vLLM and SGLang solve the same block-management problem in Python, TensorRT-LLM splits the role across MPI processes, and OpenVINO shows what one-graph-per-stream looks like without any server at all. TurboMind’s answer — one thread, one plan, pooled pages — is the most conservative and arguably the easiest to reason about under load.
entry.summary: A second source tour of InternLM/lmdeploy, this time inside the TurboMind C++ core: the Gateway that ships requests across the pybind boundary, the Engine's internal thread, the Scheduler's admission and prefix-reuse machinery, pooled logical and cache blocks, and the ModelExecutor thread that turns a BatchData into a forward pass.

entry.title: Engine Actions and the Token Treadmill - The C++ Serve Core of mlc-ai/mlc-llm

link.title: Engine Actions and the Token Treadmill - The C++ Serve Core of mlc-ai/mlc-llm

entry.content:
Our first walk of mlc-ai/mlc-llm told the compile-and-serve story at the repository scale: passes that fuse weight dequantization into matmuls, quantization schemes, the async Python engine, and a note that a compact C++ core does the real work. That C++ core is where the interesting scheduling happens, and it deserves the kind of attention TurboMind got from us in the lmdeploy follow-up. Every inference loop on the planet has the same shape — pick a batch, run prefill or decode, sample, stream deltas back — and the differences between frameworks live in how each decides what a “step” is, how requests move between queues, and what happens when you want to draft five tokens and throw four away. mlc-llm answers all three with an unusually clean vocabulary: one background thread, a step function that selects exactly one EngineAction per iteration, and a request-state machine whose draft token slots make speculative decoding a bookkeeping exercise rather than a special case. As always, this is an educational read of published Apache-2.0 source on the main branch; the first post at /mlc-llm/ covers the compiler side we deliberately skip here.

The architectural headline is that the whole serving engine is a two-thread conversation. Requests arrive from Python as instructions into a queue owned by the background thread; the background thread runs step after step, and every delta — every new token — flows back through a callback loop into Python without either thread ever blocking the other. Everything else in cpp/serve exists to keep that conversation moving: the actions are the verbs, the state is the ledger, and the sampler is the arithmetic.

Overview of the serve core: Python engines hand instructions to the ThreadedEngine, its background loop drives EngineImpl's step dispatcher, the EngineAction family covers prefill, decode, and speculative paths, EngineState and RequestState track every request, and the prefix cache plus GPU sampler close the loop.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • engine_base.py is the Python side of the callback bridge: the async stream callback turns C++ deltas into asyncio wakeups, with a sync twin at line 548.
  • sync_engine.py exposes add_request and an explicit step for callers who want to own the loop.
  • threaded_engine.cc owns RunBackgroundLoop and RunBackgroundStreamBackLoop, fed by an instruction queue at line 356.
  • engine.cc is the dispatcher: EngineImpl::Step, beside AddRequest at line 668 and HandleSpecialRequests at 535.
  • engine_state.cc keeps the queues and hands out per-request states plus the running-state list at 33.
  • action.h declares the entire action vocabulary in one line: Step takes the state and returns finished requests.
  • new_request_prefill.cc starts running requests; batch_decode.cc keeps them running one token at a time.
  • auto_spec_decode.cc routes between draft, verify, and jump-forward when a draft model is configured.
  • request_state.cc is the ledger: CommitToken, RollbackTokens at 70, AddDraftToken at 85.
  • prefix_cache.cc reuses work through ExtendSequence, RollBackSequence at 177, and RecycleSequence at 191.
  • gpu_sampler.cc does the arithmetic: top-p renormalization and batched sampling at 190.
  • logit_processor.cc shapes logits before sampling with bias, penalties, and grammar masks.

A step is an action

The design’s one big idea is easiest to see in the dispatcher. EngineImpl::Step does no model work itself: it checks whether there are new requests to absorb or dead requests to clean, picks exactly one action object, calls its Step, and hands the returned list of finished request ids to the state for cleanup. Which action gets picked is a matter of one if-chain: if any waiting request can join the batch, prefill; if a speculative configuration is active, the speculative action; otherwise decode. Each action is a self-contained class. NewRequestPrefillActionObj::Step walks the waiting queue, consults the prefix cache for reusable blocks, and packs as many prompts as fit into a chord-shaped prefill batch. BatchDecodeActionObj::Step is the treadmill’s heartbeat: it assembles the running batch, runs one forward step on the model, then samples the whole batch in one call at line 170. Underneath both, function_table.cc is the FFI registry that made the model callable: Init and _InitFunctions at 207 load the TVM runtime functions — prefill, decode, kv cache ops — that every action calls by name, and CopyToWorker0 shuttles host data to the device. Where actions need each other’s plumbing, action_commons.cc shares the batch-assembly and output-merge helpers rather than duplicating them.

The two-thread story is what makes this elegant rather than merely neat. Python calls into ThreadedEngine only to push an instruction — add request, abort request, reload — and the instruction queue at line 356 is the single crossing point. The background loop drains it, runs steps, and parks deltas in an output queue; the stream-back loop at 191 waits on that queue and fires the callback into Python. Two condition variables, no locks held during model execution, and the vtable at line 386 is the whole surface Python ever sees. It is a lighter pattern than the process-per-worker lattice we mapped in TensorRT-LLM, and it means a reload never tears down the Python event loop.

The lifecycle bookkeeping around that loop is worth its own paragraph, because it shows how much production reality the dispatcher absorbs. Engine construction is Engine::Create at line 1016, which funnels through AutoDecideEngineConfig at line 893 — the stage that fills in defaults the user left blank and picks a mode single-GPU versus speculative versus disaggregated. Requests that are not ordinary completions are intercepted before they reach the queues: HandleSpecialRequests at line 535 answers debug and control instructions inline, and HandleDisaggRequest at line 553 recognizes requests that arrived from a remote prefill node in disaggregated serving. Failures stream back through the same callback as successes — StreamBackError at line 529 wraps an error and a finish reason into a normal-looking delta so the Python side never needs a second error channel. On the far side of the bridge, process_chat_completion_request at line 687 is where OpenAI-shaped JSON becomes a C++ Request, and its stream-output twin at line 781 converts deltas back into chat-completions chunks. The wire dialect changes nothing in the core — which is precisely the point of the layering.

Speculative drafts and the state machine

Speculative decoding is where this architecture pays off. Without a draft model, a step is a decode. With one, AutoSpecDecodeActionObj::Step becomes a tiny state machine of its own: it alternates BatchDraftActionObj::Step, where the small model commits a block of k draft tokens per request, with BatchVerifyActionObj::Step, where the large model runs all drafts in parallel and the sampler accepts the longest correct prefix. A jump-forward action at line 36 handles the structured-output case — when a grammar or a JSON schema says the next five characters are already decided, the engine jumps them without a forward pass at all. The EAGLE path swaps in different actions — eagle_batch_draft.cc and eagle_batch_verify.cc — with feature vectors and tree-shaped verification, and the dispatcher at line 78 wraps whichever family you configured.

What makes draft-then-verify cheap to reason about is the request state. RequestModelStateNode::AddDraftToken parks each draft in a numbered slot; CommitToken records accepted tokens and RollbackTokens rewinds the ones the verifier rejected, with RemoveAllDraftTokens reporting which KV cache slots to recycle. The same ledger serves non-speculative paths: grammar-constrained decoding asks for a token bitmask at line 48, and every streamed delta is composed by GetDeltaRequestReturn at line 175. The sampler underneath is quietly sophisticated: BatchRenormalizeProbsByTopP renormalizes on-device before BatchSampleTokensWithProbAfterTopP at line 190 draws from the surviving mass, and GenerateUniformSamples at line 480 pre-generates random numbers on GPU so the per-request RNG state never round-trips through the host. Bias and penalties arrive earlier through InplaceUpdateLogits, UpdateWithPenalty at 270, and UpdateWithMask at 372.

The prefix cache underneath

Serving quality often depends on what you do not recompute, and this repo’s answer is a paged radix tree in C++. PrefixCacheImpl exposes four operations: ExtendSequence claims blocks for growing tokens, CommitSequenceExtention at 154 makes a speculative extension durable, RollBackSequence at 177 releases the tail after verification rewinds, and RecycleSequence at 191 marks a finished conversation for lazy reuse. The tree itself, radix_tree.cc, indexes sequences at block granularity so two conversations sharing a system prompt share those KV blocks for free — the same idea we saw in SGLang’s radix cache and in the Python-side tree the first tour showed, now living close to the C++ actions that use it. TryFreeMemory at line 225 is the pressure valve that evicts leaves when a new prefill needs room.

From Install to Your First Model

None of this needs configuration: python -m mlc_llm serve builds it and runs it, and create_sync or AsyncThreadedEngine expose the same core in-process. The visible knobs are speculative — a draft model plus spec decode mode flips the action dispatcher — and the debug surface: the event trace recorder emits per-request spans you can read in Chrome’s trace viewer, which is the fastest way to see the prefill-chord and draft-verify alternation in a real log.

Honest limits: we read the single-GPU path; disaggregated prefill and decode across nodes exists in the same actions folder but we did not trace it, and the embedding engine shares none of this. The sampler reads correct but we benchmarked nothing — top-p behavior on GPU is exactly where silent numerical drift hides. And the action set is still growing; jump-forward and EAGLE both landed recently, which is why this layer rewards a second reading. For context: vLLM solves speculative decoding at the Python scheduler layer, SGLang shares the radix-tree idea from the same lineage, LM Studio-style local stacks wrap engines rather than reimplement them, and LocalAI routes to backends it does not own. mlc-llm’s one-action-per-step C++ core is the most legible of these — you can hold the whole token treadmill in your head, which is exactly why it was worth a second visit.
entry.summary: A second source tour of mlc-ai/mlc-llm, this time inside the C++ serve core: the ThreadedEngine's two background loops, EngineImpl's step dispatcher, the EngineAction family from prefill to decode to speculative draft and verify, the request state machine with its draft slots and rollbacks, the GPU sampler's top-p machinery, and the radix-tree prefix cache underneath.

entry.title: From Run() to Buffers - The ONNX Runtime Execution Machinery

link.title: From Run() to Buffers - The ONNX Runtime Execution Machinery

entry.content:
Our first walk of microsoft/onnxruntime stayed at the architectural level: the versioned C API, the fusion transformers, MLAS, the CUDA provider, and the training stack. That post ends where every session ends up on a hot path — a call to Run() with a dictionary of feeds — and leaves the most performance-critical half of the codebase unexplored: what actually happens between that call and the last kernel’s write. This tour follows exactly that half. It is a story with three distinct layers. At the top, InferenceSession::RunImpl validates options and hands the plan to an executor. In the middle, ExecuteThePlan walks the graph across a small set of device streams, checking barriers before each node fires. At the bottom, an ExecutionFrame and a best-fit-coalescing arena have already pre-computed — at session initialization time — where every byte of every intermediate tensor will live, so that a steady-state inference run performs almost no allocator decision-making at all. As always in this series, this is an educational read of published MIT-licensed source on the main branch; the first post at /onnxruntime/ covers the API surface and provider layer that this machinery serves.

The headline is that ONNX Runtime treats allocation as a compile-time problem, not a runtime one. Two planners run during Initialize, not during inference: one assigns nodes and weights to devices, the other traces every buffer’s lifetime and folds the resulting sizes into reusable memory patterns. By the time Run() is called, the expensive questions have yes-or-no answers cached in the session state, and the per-run work reduces to bookkeeping — which is why the code can afford a comparatively elegant stream walk in the middle.

Overview of the execution machinery: RunImpl enters the executor, ExecuteThePlan walks nodes through the StreamExecutionContext and DeviceStreamCollection down to device handles like CudaStream, the planners and ExecutionFrame pre-compute every allocation into the BFCArena, and KernelRegistryManager plus the Memcpy kernel and the ThreadPool round out the launch path.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • inference_session.cc is the public face: Load for file paths, RunImpl for the hot path, and RunAsync at 4141 for the callback variant.
